name: Monk strap shoes

lead: A monk strap shoe is a dress shoe that fastens with one or two buckled straps rather than laces. It sits between an Oxford and a Derby in formality, so it dresses up chinos or jeans and works with a suit.

The appearance payoff is style: a clean silhouette with a visible buckle detail that reads as deliberate and put together. It comes in single-strap and double-strap versions, often with a cap toe, and is popular in suede as well as polished leather.

paras: People wear them with tailored trousers, suits and smart casual outfits, choosing single-strap for a cleaner look and double monks for a bolder one. They need no laces, so they go on quickly, and care is the same as for other leather shoes: brushing, polish and shoe trees.
There are no health risks beyond ordinary footwear fit. New leather dress shoes can need breaking in, and the buckle fit depends on the instep, so sizing and try-on matter.

chain: Adds a distinctive, polished detail and mid-level formality
angle.text: Monk strap shoes change how a smart outfit reads by adding a visible buckle detail and a dress-shoe shape that suits suits and smart casual wear alike.

lead: A monk shoe, or monk strap, is a laceless dress shoe secured by one or more buckles and straps [1]. Wikipedia attributes the innovation of the style to English shoemaker Edward Green in the late 19th century [1].

The main versions are the single-strap monk and the double monk. Monk shoes often have a cap toe, are sometimes brogued, and are popular in suede [1]. In formality they are described as less formal than an Oxford but more formal than a Derby, and some fashion specialists call the monk the most accomplished men's dress shoe [1].

For someone improving how they dress, the shoe is a way to finish an outfit: the buckle adds a focal detail at the foot while keeping the formality of a dress shoe. The Wall Street Journal listed the monk strap among essential men's items in 2014 and wrote about the double monk's return as a trend in 2023, according to Wikipedia's sources [1].
infobox: One or two buckled straps, no laces
Late 19th century, credited to Edward Green (England)

paras: The defining feature is the closure: straps that cross the vamp and fasten with buckles in place of lacing [1]. The single monk has one strap and the double monk has two. Cap toes and broguing are common, and suede versions are popular [1].

Wikipedia credits English shoemaker Edward Green with innovating the style in the late 19th century, without giving an exact year [1]. Press coverage in the Wall Street Journal in 2014 and 2023 placed the shoe among men's wardrobe essentials and described the double monk's resurgence [1].
Because the monk is more formal than a Derby and less formal than an Oxford, it is used across a range of outfits, from suits to casual trousers [1].
